question: On the Genesis sound chip the sixth music voice and the drum channel are the same piece of hardware, so a song can only have one of them at a time. The engine's driver already supports three different ways to share it, and it picks one per song. Seraph has no way for a song to say which one it was written for, so the app always plays drums and the sixth voice together. That is right for one of the three ways and wrong for the other two, and it is wrong silently: the song sounds fuller in the app than it will in the game.

options.name: Always play it the way where drums borrow the voice and give it back
options.what: Preview matches the most common of the three ways. A drum hit briefly interrupts the sixth voice and the melody resumes after it, exactly as the game does in that mode.
options.costs: About half a day. Songs written the other way, where the sixth voice is given up for good, will still sound better in the app than in the game. That is the same wrong promise, just narrower.

options.name: Let each song say which of the three ways it uses
options.what: The app is right for all three. Preview, the overlap warnings and every export follow whatever the song says, and a song written for one way cannot be quietly played back as another.
options.costs: Several days. It adds a permanent setting to the song file, so existing songs need converting when they open, and each of the three export paths has to be taught to carry it.

options.name: Change nothing, and mark the places where the game will differ
options.what: Playback stays exactly as it is today. Anywhere drums and the sixth voice sound at once, the app flags it so you can see what the game will not deliver.
options.costs: About a day. The app still plays something the game cannot, so your ears are still being told the wrong thing while your eyes are told the right one.

recommend.because: The two cheaper options are each correct for some songs and quietly wrong for the rest, and the whole reason this came up is that a quiet wrong answer in playback is the expensive kind. The cost is also more spread out than it looks: the setting can ship with a sensible default and no controls at all, which makes playback honest straight away, and the controls and export work can follow once you have heard which way you actually write in.

detail: F27. Seraph's preview keeps the DAC as an independent stream summed into the mix and never writes register $2B; aeon's driver writes $2B at four sites and has a three mode per song ch6 contract (DEDICATE / FM6-FM / ADAPTIVE), verified firsthand at aeon origin/master 139995f2. The always-steal option is right in ADAPTIVE and actively wrong in FM6-FM, where the voice loss is permanent. Full grounding in docs/superpowers/2026-08-21-daw-feel-audit.md, section 'F27 GROUNDED 2026-08-23'. F31 (the driver profile advertising seven voices on a six voice chip) is upstream of this and wrong however it resolves.

question: On the Genesis sound chip the sixth music voice and the drum channel are the same piece of hardware, so a song can only have one of them at a time. The engine's driver already supports three different ways to share it, and it picks one per song. Seraph has no way for a song to say which one it was written for, so the app always plays drums and the sixth voice together. That is right for one of the three ways and wrong for the other two, and it is wrong silently: the song sounds fuller in the app than it will in the game. You asked whether the engine should just determine this, on the reasoning that if a given driver always eats a voice for drums then a song on that driver should behave that way. Checking it against the drivers already read here: you are right, and more strongly than the question was written. Of the five drivers whose actual bytes were read, every one turns drums off when no sample is playing and not one of them lets the sixth voice and drums sound at the same time. The Sonic 3 driver does not even have a sixth music voice to lose. Your own engine is the only one found that offers a choice.

options.name: Let the engine decide, because the engine already does
options.what: Each driver carries its own answer and Seraph follows it. Pick the Sonic 3 driver and the sixth voice is simply not a music voice, because in that driver it does not exist. Pick a driver that hands the voice back after each drum hit and playback does that. Nothing is set per song, and a song cannot be written against a rule its driver does not have.
options.costs: The driver descriptions in the app have to become right first, and today there is one and it is wrong: it offers seven voices on a chip that has six. Roughly two days for the descriptions plus wiring playback to them. Your own engine is the one case this does not fully answer, because it genuinely supports three behaviours and picks per song, so it still needs one setting later. Every other driver read needs none.

options.name: Always play it the way where drums borrow the voice and give it back
options.what: Preview matches the most common of the three ways. A drum hit briefly interrupts the sixth voice and the melody resumes after it, exactly as the game does in that mode.
options.costs: About half a day. Songs written the other way, where the sixth voice is given up for good, will still sound better in the app than in the game. That is the same wrong promise, just narrower.

options.name: Let each song say which of the three ways it uses
options.what: The app is right for all three. Preview, the overlap warnings and every export follow whatever the song says, and a song written for one way cannot be quietly played back as another.
options.costs: Several days. It adds a permanent setting to the song file, so existing songs need converting when they open, and each of the three export paths has to be taught to carry it.

options.name: Change nothing, and mark the places where the game will differ
options.what: Playback stays exactly as it is today. Anywhere drums and the sixth voice sound at once, the app flags it so you can see what the game will not deliver.
options.costs: About a day. The app still plays something the game cannot, so your ears are still being told the wrong thing while your eyes are told the right one.

recommend.because: It is the cheapest of the four and the only one that cannot be authored wrong, because a song never gets to claim a behaviour its driver does not have. It also reverses what needs doing first: fixing the driver descriptions stops being tidying up and becomes the actual fix, and that work is already sitting next in the queue. The one gap is your own engine, which really does support three behaviours per song, so a single setting is still wanted there later. That is a much smaller thing than adding the setting to every song in the app, and it can wait until you have heard which way you write.

detail: F27, superseding d-1 per rule 8b: this option is his, added rather than mapped onto the nearest one already offered, and the wording of what it buys follows his framing. EVIDENCE, from docs/research/2026-08-23-f27-driver-truth.md section 2, which read paired .lst disassemblies rather than trusting in-repo analyses. S3K Flamedriver: zSongFM6_DAC is one track slot and the init table literally comments 'FM6 music track (does not exist in this driver)'. Batman: allocation level exclusion, channel 5 skipped per sub-frame whenever the sample-active flag is set. Alien Storm, Gunstar, TF4: per sample $2B edge, TF4 through a helper with the register in h, which is why a naive grep reads as never writing it. MDSDRV, second hand and marked as such: slot 5 is FM6-or-PCM1, one voice id, so the format cannot express both. Section 2.3: nobody lets FM6 and the DAC sound simultaneously and no driver read represents that state at all. CAVEAT ON HIS EXAMPLE, stated rather than glossed: Sonic 1 specifically was NOT among the blobs read. The five read were Batman, Alien Storm, Gunstar, TF4 and S3K. His instinct holds across all five; S1 itself is untested here. CONSEQUENCE: this promotes F31 from cleanup to the first step of the fix. Seraph's only DriverProfile is FlamedriverProfile, it advertises six FM voices including FM6/DAC plus a separate DAC channel, seven voices on a six voice chip, and there is no aeon/Memra profile at all. Under this option the profile is the thing that carries the answer, so it has to be right before anything reads it.

That is a real objection to what I recommended last time and it changes my recommendation.

options.costs: A little extra care up front, roughly a day, and it is a promise that has to be kept honestly rather than assumed.

options.name: Wait until your own engine's driver stops moving, then build against it
options.what: Your idea, recorded as you put it rather than folded into one of the others. Nothing gets designed against a target that is still shifting, so no part of the foundation has to be redone when the engine settles.
options.costs: Everything on this app's main line stops until the engine is close to final, and that date is not in anyone's hands right now because the engine is mid migration. The defect work here does not need the foundation and would carry on, so this is a stall rather than an idle lane, but the main line is a stall of unknown length. It also does not fix the thing that actually makes a foundation wrong, since a foundation shaped around one driver is shaped around one driver whether or not that driver is finished.

options.name: Two drivers, deliberately as different as possible, and not four
options.what: Build the foundation against your engine's driver and exactly one established driver chosen for being its opposite, rather than against four. The evidence already sitting in this repo says S3K is that opposite: it has no sixth music voice at all, where your engine is the only driver found anywhere that lets a song choose. A shape that can describe both of those honestly can describe the ones in between, and the established half is frozen, so the shape gets tested against something that cannot shift under it.
options.costs: One extra driver studied rather than three, so days rather than a week, and it is still more than following the plan on file. If the pair turns out not to span enough, a third driver is added later against a shape that has already been forced to generalise once, which is much cheaper than the first generalisation.

recommend.because: Your instinct to go to the established drivers was right, and for a stronger reason than the one you gave, which is why waiting is not the answer. Drift in your own engine is the cheap problem: the foundation reads the engine's numbers out of its source every time rather than copying them, so when the engine moves those numbers move with it. The expensive problem is the shape, meaning what a channel is and how a driver declares what it does, and a shape drawn around one driver quietly assumes that driver. Waiting pays an open ended delay and still leaves you with a shape drawn around one driver, so it fixes the cheap problem and not the expensive one. Two things already point the same way. Your own channel six ruling says the driver carries the behaviour and the app follows it, which only means anything if the format can express drivers that behave differently. And the research already here read five drivers and found five different answers, with your engine the odd one out as the only one offering a per song choice, so it is the least representative example to draw the shape around. Two contrasting drivers get you that test for roughly a quarter of the work of four, and the established half cannot shift while you build against it.

question: Saving a song out as a VGM file (the format a music player or a sharing site reads) currently throws away every drum, and until today it did that without saying a word. I have made it say so, and it now warns you by name which drum tracks were left out. Whether I should go further and make it actually export the drums is your call, because it is a bigger job than it looks and there is a reason it may not be worth doing yet. Drums in a VGM are not a setting that gets written once. They are a stream of individual sound samples that has to be woven, moment by moment, in among every other instrument's notes, which means rebuilding the part of the export that decides what happens when. The thing that changes the answer: nothing in the app can produce a VGM at all right now. The button was never wired up, so the code is reachable only from inside the program itself.

options.name: Build proper drum export into VGM now
options.what: VGM files come out complete, with percussion, the moment the export button is wired up.
options.costs: Several days of the kind of work that is easy to get subtly wrong, on a feature nothing can currently reach. The timing has to be right by ear, so you would owe me a listening pass at the end before it could be trusted.

options.name: Do it as part of wiring up the export button, not before
options.what: The drum work happens when the button is actually connected, so the first VGM anyone can produce is complete on the first try. Nothing ships drumless because nothing ships until then.
options.costs: The warning I added today is what protects you in the meantime, and it only protects you if it is read. If the button gets wired up by someone who ignores it, a drumless VGM escapes.

options.name: Leave VGM music only, permanently, and keep the warning
options.what: No further work. VGM stays a way to share the melodic part of a song; the route that actually reaches your game is the other export, which handles drums separately.
options.costs: Anyone you send a VGM to hears the song with no percussion. If VGM is how you intend to share music, this is the wrong answer.

recommend.because: The gap costs you nothing today, and I checked that rather than assuming it: the export button is not connected to anything, so no VGM can currently leave the app by any route you have. Doing several days of delicate timing work on a feature nobody can reach spends your time at the worst possible moment, and it would need a listening pass from you at the end, which is your time too. Doing it when the button is wired means the very first VGM anyone can make is already right, which is the outcome the original finding was worried about. The one real risk is that the warning gets ignored by whoever wires the button, so I have gated that work behind this in the queue and said why in the code at the exact spot the drums are dropped.

detail: F29. export_vgm_data had ChannelAssignment::Dac(_) => continue, dropping every DAC track before reading a note, and export_vgm returned a bare byte count. Landed today (merge fd6d21b): export_vgm_data now returns VgmExport { data, skipped_dac_tracks } and the command appends a warning naming the tracks. Three tests, poisoned red-first, two of them controls against the inverse defect. NOT landed: actual DAC representation, which needs a 0x67 PCM data block plus 0x8n write-and-wait commands interleaved sample-accurately with FM and PSG events, i.e. restructuring the tick-based event loop in export_vgm_data into a sample-accurate one. Sizing therefore corrected from the booked M to L. Dead-UI-path claim verified firsthand this session, not taken from the README-7 booking: exportVgm exists in src/bindings.ts and src/api/ipc.ts but no component calls it. Interaction worth noting: a faithful DAC export must write register $2B, whose semantics are F27's parked design call, but F31 landing first removed the conflict for new songs since Flamedriver now correctly offers no FM6 music voice; only a legacy song carrying an Fm(5) track still hits it.
